title: Count the Different Substrings

concept.title: Every block gets a key, equal keys are one substring
body: Comparing two blocks of a word letter by letter costs as much as their length. A **polynomial rolling hash** turns every block into a number in O(1) after one preparation pass. Treat the letters as digits of a number in some base `B` (modulo a big prime `M`): `hash(s[l..r)) = s[l]*B^(r-l-1) + ... + s[r-1]`.

body.code:
h[i + 1] = (h[i] * B + value(s[i])) % M        # prefix hashes, one pass
block(l, r) = (h[r] - h[l] * B^(r - l)) % M       # O(1) for any block

body: Equal blocks always have equal hashes. Different blocks have different hashes with very high probability, and using **two moduli at once** makes a collision practically impossible (the two values are packed into one 62-bit number). With such keys, blocks can be put into hash sets and compared in O(1).

A word of length `n` has `n * (n + 1) / 2` blocks, but many of them are equal. Give **every block** its key and count the **different keys**: put them all in a set, or write them into an array, sort it and count the runs of equal numbers.

Storing the blocks themselves as strings would need `O(n^3)` memory. Storing one 62-bit number per block needs only `O(n^2)` numbers, which is the reason to use hashing here. (Suffix structures count them even faster, but this method is the simplest to write.)

statement: Count the different non-empty substrings (blocks of consecutive letters) of a word. Two blocks that consist of the same letters in the same order count as one substring, wherever they are in the word.
inputFormat: A single word of lowercase letters.
outputFormat: Print the number of different substrings.

examples.note: The different substrings are a, b, ab, ba, aba, bab and abab: 7.

hints: Every block `s[i..j)` needs a key that is cheap to compute: use a rolling hash.
Collect the keys of all blocks of all lengths.
The answer is the number of different keys (a set, or sort and count runs).

explanation: Every block has a rolling-hash key; the number of different keys is the number of different substrings.

code.python:
M1, M2 = 1000000007, 998244353
B1, B2 = 911382323, 972663749


def build_hash(s):
    n = len(s)
    h1 = [0] * (n + 1)
    h2 = [0] * (n + 1)
    p1 = [1] * (n + 1)
    p2 = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        v = ord(ch) - 96
        h1[i + 1] = (h1[i] * B1 + v) % M1
        h2[i + 1] = (h2[i] * B2 + v) % M2
        p1[i + 1] = p1[i] * B1 % M1
        p2[i + 1] = p2[i] * B2 % M2
    return h1, h2, p1, p2


def sub_key(hash_data, l, r):
    h1, h2, p1, p2 = hash_data
    a = (h1[r] - h1[l] * p1[r - l]) % M1
    b = (h2[r] - h2[l] * p2[r - l]) % M2
    return a * M2 + b

s = input().strip()

n = len(s)
data = build_hash(s)
seen = set()
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i + 1, n + 1):
        seen.add(sub_key(data, i, j))
print(len(seen))
